chunks: Among what the Shaykh, may Allah the Exalted support him, informed me of, he said:

Abu al-Qasim Ja'far ibn Muhammad informed me, from Muhammad ibn Ya'qub, from a number of our companions, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Shadhan ibn al-Khalil al-Naysaburi, from Ma'mar ibn 'Umar, from Abu Ja'far عليه السلام, who said:
"For wiping the head, the area of three fingers suffices, and likewise the foot."
If it is said: How can you rely on this report when the apparent meaning of the Qur'an seems to reject it, because Allah the Exalted said:

(1) And the letter ba' here is for attachment, and it only entered to connect the wiping to the heads, not to indicate partiality, because its indicating partiality is not found in the speech of the Arabs. If that is so, then the apparent sense requires wiping the whole head. It is said to them: Our companions have inferred from this verse that wiping in the case of the head and the two feet is with part of them, because they said: It is established that the ba' has various functions in speech: sometimes it enters for addition and attachment, and sometimes it enters for partiality. It is not permissible to carry it upon addition and attachment except where necessary, because the true place of speech is specifically for benefit, especially when it proceeds from one who is wise and knowing; by this it is distinguished from the speech of one inattentive, sleeping, or rambling. Also, the ba' only enters for attachment in a place where the verb does not itself pass over to the object, such as their saying, 'I passed by Zayd' and 'I went with 'Amr,' for passing and going do not themselves govern an object directly, so the ba' entered to connect the two verbs to the two objects. But when the verb is of the sort that governs by itself and does not need the ba' for transitivity, and we find that they have inserted the ba' upon it, we know that they inserted it because of an additional benefit that was not otherwise there, and that is partiality. And His saying, Exalted is He:

is of the sort in which the verb governs by itself. Do you not see that if He had said, 'Wipe your heads,' the speech would have been complete in itself and meaningful? Therefore, the entry of the ba' in this place must carry a renewed benefit, according to what we have mentioned, and it is nothing other than partiality. For whenever we carry it upon what the opponents have held, namely attachment and addition, then its presence and absence would be equal, and this is vainness, which is not permissible regarding Allah the Exalted. If it is said: Allah the Exalted has also said in the verse of tayammum:
"Then wipe your faces and your hands."

(1) then it should follow that wiping is with part of the face. We say: That is indeed what we hold, because according to us wiping in tayammum is obligatory with part of the face, namely the forehead and the two eyebrows. And the report indicates that the ba' entails partiality.

key_terms.التَّبْعِيضُ: partiality, meaning that only part of a thing is intended
key_terms.التَّيَمُّمِ: tayammum (dry ablution), cited as a parallel Qur'anic case
key_terms.الرَّأْسِ: the head, the body part to be wiped in wudu (ablution)
key_terms.الرِّجْلُ: the foot, likewise subject to wiping in this report
key_terms.الْإِلْصَاقِ: attachment or direct connection, the alternative grammatical meaning debated here
key_terms.الْبَاءُ: the Arabic preposition under discussion for its legal and linguistic implication
key_terms.الْخَبَرِ: the report or hadith used as evidence
key_terms.مَسْحِ: wiping, the ritual act discussed in wudu (ablution) and tayammum

ai.seo_question: Does the Qur'an require wiping the entire head in wudu (ablution), or is wiping part of it sufficient?
ai.summary: This passage presents a hadith from Abu Ja'far عليه السلام stating that wiping an area equal to three fingers on the head, and likewise on the foot, suffices in wudu (ablution). It then argues, through linguistic analysis of the Qur'anic wording, that the preposition in "وَامْسَحُوا بِرُءُوسِكُمْ" indicates wiping part of the head rather than all of it, and extends this reasoning to tayammum as well.
